Appendix A Discussion: Scope, Limitations, and Broader Impact

This appendix articulates the scope of evaluative claims our benchmark supports (§A.1), identifies five categories of limitations and their downstream effects (§A.2), proposes four research directions through which the framework can be extended (§A.3), discusses societal and engineering implications (§A.4), and positions VM relative to adjacent failure modes (§A.5).

A.1 Scope and Operational Assumptions

Construct.

Verified Misguidance (VM) refers to the structural condition under which a citation-bearing answer may mislead users despite the cited source being real, accessible, and faithfully cited, a condition distinct from hallucination [24]. We operationalize this as the simultaneous failure of three structurally distinct axes: query intent–source purpose alignment, answer–source fidelity, and source-type suitability for the domain. The three dimensions capture statistically independent failure modes; as Appendix C.4 shows, single-dimension failures dwarf joint failures by an order of magnitude, so a single-dimension evaluation framework would miss the structural patterns we report.

Supported claims.

CiteTrace supports three claim types: existence, that citation pairs failing all three dimensions are measurable and non-degenerate within our setting (28 communities, 10 models, English, March–April 2026); comparison, that ranking-level differences across models, providers, and domains are robust (Appendix D.4, D.6); and diagnosis, identifying which axis fails individually and how the three co-fail (Appendix D.3–D.4). We do not support claims of permanent provider quality, generalization to non-English settings, or causal isolation of retrieval versus generation.

Measurement assumptions.

Five assumptions support our measurements; each is paired with a corresponding limitation in §A.2.

  • A1

    Citation-marker semantics. We interpret each provider’s citation marker as asserting source–answer grounding, consistent with all five providers’ API documentation (Appendix B.2).

  • A2

    Predefined-matrix validity. IPA and SS matrices are expert-designed instruments; rankings remain stable under cell-wise ±1\pm 1 perturbations (Appendix C.3, D.6).

  • A3

    LLM-judge reliability. GPT-4o-mini’s per-dimension κ\kappa (0.7880.788–0.8790.879) meets the Landis–Koch substantial-agreement threshold [33]; three-annotator human validation (Krippendorff α≥0.811\alpha\geq 0.811 [30]) supports taxonomy stability (Appendix C).

  • A4

    Query representativeness. Stack Exchange Q&A represents one dimension of real-world information needs; we make no claim about conversational or multi-turn search.

  • A5

    Temporal snapshot. Results reflect a 15-day window; we do not claim trends outside this window.

A.2 Limitations

We acknowledge five categories of limitations that bound the interpretation of our findings, pairing each with its downstream effect.

Crawl-failure coverage bias.

36.8% of cited URLs failed to crawl, with failures concentrated on Forum/Q&A (67.9%) and Social/Blog (55.0%) hosts due to Cloudflare bot blocking (Appendix D.6). The downstream metrics (AFR, SFR, FFR) are computed only over successfully crawled citations and therefore exclude these failures from the denominator; we estimate that including failed pages would raise YMYL SFR by 7–9 percentage points beyond the reported 27.1%. Future work could supplement live crawling with archival snapshots (e.g., the Internet Archive) for bot-blocked URLs.

LLM-as-Judge dependence.

All taxonomy classifications and fidelity adjudication share a single LLM dependency (GPT-4o-mini), which may propagate systematic biases into downstream metrics in ways not fully captured by aggregate κ\kappa. This single-judge design follows the established methodology of comparable frameworks (ALCE [16] validates against a single NLI model, RAGAS [14] prompts a single LLM, and ARES [47] trains one judge per dimension), and our per-dimension κ\kappa (0.788–0.879) substantially exceeds their reported agreement levels. We further mitigate single-judge risk through an explicit UNEVALUABLE escape label that removes ambiguous cases from the evaluation pool (Appendix B.3). Nonetheless, absolute values may shift under judge replacement; we report relative cross-model and cross-provider patterns as the primary claims and encourage replication with an alternative judge family.

Predefined-matrix subjectivity.

The IPA and SS matrices are expert-designed instruments rather than data-derived scores. ICC [28] and threshold-sensitivity analyses confirm rank stability under cell-wise ±1\pm 1 perturbations (Kendall τ≥0.82\tau\geq 0.82 in five of seven variants), but reasonable experts may assign different scores to specific cells. A more ambitious extension would elicit cell values from a structured panel of 20–50 experts per domain, allowing publication of a probabilistic version of each matrix.

Linguistic and cultural scope.

CiteTrace’s 11,200 queries are drawn from English-language Stack Exchange. Information-asymmetry dynamics may differ in non-English contexts where the commercial-source landscape, regulatory environment, and platform ecosystems differ; for example, in markets with prominent state-affiliated media or single-platform Q&A communities (Naver Knowledge-iN, Zhihu), our SP/ST taxonomies may need refinement. We view cross-cultural extension (§A.3) as a high-priority direction.

Temporal snapshot and causal attribution.

Each provider’s search tool issues live web queries, so identical prompts may return different sources at different times. We minimize variation through a 15-day collection window, with all axes within ±5 percentage points across the window’s two halves (Appendix D.6), but full reproducibility is not attainable. Our framework also characterizes where VM concentrates but does not isolate which pipeline stage (retrieval, generation, or interaction) produces it. Controlled experiments with fixed retrieval or fixed generation would enable sharper causal decomposition; this is currently blocked by the closed-source nature of commercial retrieval pipelines.

A.3 Future Directions

The limitations above suggest four concrete research directions.

Multilingual and cross-cultural extension.

Extending CiteTrace to non-English Stack Exchange and to non-Stack-Exchange platforms (Zhihu, Naver Knowledge-iN, Reddit) would test whether VM concentrates on the same domain–source-type combinations across cultures and whether the 88–96% provider variance dominance holds when search backends are tuned to non-English markets.

Longitudinal observation.

A quarterly variant (CiteTrace-Longitudinal) re-issuing the same 11,200 queries would track whether absolute FFR/SFR/AFR levels are improving, whether cross-provider trade-offs persist, and whether YMYL-domain failures narrow under retrieval-policy updates. The marginal collection cost is modest, and the result is a continuous monitoring signal that single-shot benchmarks cannot provide.

Causal decomposition through controlled retrieval.

A controlled experiment with the retrieved-context set held fixed while the generator is varied (and vice versa) would isolate the contribution of each pipeline stage, moving from descriptive characterization (where does VM concentrate?) to mechanistic understanding (which pipeline stage produces it?).

Mitigation-oriented benchmarking.

Three concrete mitigation paths follow from our findings: intent-aware retrieval reranking (inverting IPA matrix as a scoring function), domain-aware source filtering for YMYL (given the 2.3-fold Fisher OR), and citation-quality nudging at generation time (since reasoning models reduce FFR but not SFR). We release the framework, matrices, and per-citation labels to support replication of these mitigation experiments.

A.4 Broader Impact

Societal implications: misguidance at scale.

Search-augmented LLMs increasingly mediate access to information in high-stakes decision-making domains. Hundreds of millions of users now consult these systems in lieu of traditional search engines [38], treating the presence of a citation as a sufficient guarantee of accuracy [13]. Our work demonstrates empirically that this trust is not always warranted: 30.6% of citations distort their sources, 27.1% originate from domain-inappropriate sources, and at the response level up to 90% of users encounter at least one such citation. Unlike a hallucinated fact, a citation-bearing answer that is faithful to a structurally inappropriate source presents no surface signal that distinguishes it from a trustworthy one; at scale, even single-digit failure rates translate into millions of misguidance events per day in the YMYL domains where misguidance carries the highest cost.

Implications for AI evaluation and system design.

Our cross-dimension analysis (Appendix C.4) shows that a system can score well on any single citation-quality dimension while failing structurally on another: ALCE-style citation precision [16] and RAGAS-style faithfulness [14] target answer-source fidelity, while CRAAP- and SourceBench-style source quality [8, 25] target source suitability, and neither captures their interaction. CiteTrace is designed to support multi-dimension structural evaluation in which a system’s citation behavior is reported as a profile across IPA, SS, and ASF rather than a scalar. For practitioners, our finding that 88–96% of citation-quality variance is provider-level (Appendix D.4) implies that retrieval-backend choice matters more than generator choice for citation quality, and that fidelity (Answer–Source Fidelity) and source-selection (Query–Source Alignment and Source Suitability) require separate engineering efforts.

Responsibility in model comparison.

Our work reports systematic differences across providers, including ranking reversals between fidelity and source suitability. These differences reflect specific model versions during a specific collection period and are not permanent properties of any provider; search-augmented systems evolve on weekly timescales, and the rankings may invert within a quarter. We release model identifiers and collection dates alongside all results to discourage citation of our rankings as static characterizations.

Ethics, safeguards, and misuse risk.

All queries derive from the Stack Exchange Data Dump (CC BY-SA 4.0), and we comply with attribution requirements. Source crawling respects robots.txt and rate limits (Appendix B.3); the public release contains URLs and metadata only, not source bodies (Appendix E.1); no human-subjects data are collected. In principle, content producers could reverse-engineer IPA matrix to boost their pages’ search-result visibility. We assess this risk as low because IPA matrix is a diagnostic tool, not a retrieval signal used by any production system.

A.5 Comparison to Adjacent Failure Modes

VM occupies a position adjacent to several phenomena studied in the LLM evaluation literature, and distinguishing it from each is essential for interpreting our findings.

Hallucination.

Hallucination [24] concerns claims that are factually false or unsupported by any source. VM is structurally distinct: by construction, the cited source in a VM instance is real and accessible, and the cited claim need not be false. The structural failure lies in alignment of source purpose to query intent (Intent–Purpose Alignment) or in source-type suitability for the domain (Source Suitability), not in factual accuracy per se. Empirically, ASF1 (Fabricated) cases (closest to classical hallucination) account for 24.5% of citations, while structural failures on IPA or SS without fabrication add roughly another 2020 percentage points.

Citation-precision benchmarks.

ALCE [16], AutoAIS [9], and related work measure whether each cited claim is supported by the cited source. This corresponds to a portion of our Answer–Source Fidelity (ASF), but treats the suitability of the cited source as exogenous: if the source supports the claim, the citation is counted as correct, regardless of whether the source is structurally suitable for the user’s intent. Our cross-dimension trade-off (Anthropic high-ASF/low-SS versus OpenAI low-ASF/high-SS) shows precisely why this is insufficient.

Source-quality benchmarks.

SourceBench [25], the CRAAP test [8], and related work evaluate the absolute quality of retrieved sources with a universal rubric, scoring each source independently of how its type interacts with its content domain. Our SS matrix (Appendix C.2) explicitly encodes this interaction: the same Wiki/Forum type is rated SS 55 when the source falls in Code/Data and SS 11 when it falls in Medical. A benchmark that ignores the domain–type interaction would conflate these cases and miss the YMYL-specific failure pattern that drives much of our reported SFR (38.3%38.3\% in YMYL versus 21.1%21.1\% outside).

Information asymmetry and trust calibration.

Our work inherits the information-asymmetry frame of 2, 4 but operationalizes it for the search-augmented LLM setting, where the LLM rather than the user is the proximate consumer of search results, and the user receives a summary that hides the structural mismatch from view. Recent trust-calibration research [38] shows that citation count raises user trust regardless of whether citations support the claim; our work contributes the system-side measurement that complements this user-side finding, quantifying the gap between surface citation behavior and the three structural quality axes.

Appendix B CiteTrace: Dataset Construction

This appendix details the dataset construction procedure summarized in Section 2. We describe how we source queries from Stack Exchange (§B.1), collect search-augmented responses and extract citations (§B.2), and crawl and filter cited sources (§B.3).

B.1 Sourcing Real-World Queries from Stack Exchange Communities

Site selection.

Stack Exchange Network [54], based on its December 31, 2025 snapshot, hosts 182+182{+} communities. We narrow this pool to 2828 sites through a four-stage selection process designed to retain communities where commercial information asymmetry is structurally possible. Stage 0 (candidate pool, 182+182{+} down to 4848) excludes communities that are unsuitable for studying commercial citation bias on substantive grounds: single-correct-answer domains (e.g., math, codegolf), fiction and entertainment sites lacking decision-making contexts (gaming, anime, movies), language-correction sites without commercial actors (english, ell), platform-specific tools dominated by a single ecosystem (emacs, tex, blender), religious-doctrine sites whose claims resist factual verification (christianity, islam), sites lacking a structural commercial-bias mechanism (lifehacks, history), and beta sites with fewer than ten thousand valid questions. The full exclusion criteria appear in Table 1. Stages 1–3 (4848 down to 2828) apply five sequential gates summarized in Table 2: requirement of expert knowledge (C1), presence of commercial actors with incentive to distort answers (C2), connection to substantive decisions (C3), distinctness of the commercial-bias mechanism across selected sites (C4), and data sufficiency after quality filtering (C5). Criterion C1 is satisfied by all 4848 Stage 0 candidates by construction; C2–C3 remove three sites with absent or unverified commercial actors (interpersonal, philosophy, ux); C4 deduplicates eight sites that share an existing site’s bias mechanism; and C5 removes nine sites whose post-filter pool falls below 400400 queries, following CQADupStack’s per-site minimum-threshold convention [19]. The remaining 2828 sites map directly to Stack Exchange’s official six-category taxonomy: Technology 55, Science 77, Life & Arts 77, Culture & Recreation 66, Professional 22, Business 11. We follow PRISM’s [27] approach of adopting an external taxonomy (UN subregion in their case) to avoid imposing our own categorization.

Quality filtering and sampling.

A five-step filter applied to all 2828 sites yields a final pool of 471,876471{,}876 eligible queries from 25,483,55525{,}483{,}555 raw posts, a 98.1%98.1\% reduction summarized stage-by-stage in Table 3. The single largest reduction is the community-validation gate (Score ≥5\geq 5, 90.96%90.96\% drop), which removes unanswered or low-quality posts; the recency gate (≥2018−01−01\geq 2018{-}01{-}01, 78.91%78.91\% drop) further restricts the pool to queries posed within the search-augmented LLM era. We then apply uniform per-site sampling of 400400 queries to obtain the final 11,20011{,}200-query dataset (28×40028\times 400). Uniform sampling is essential because Stack Overflow alone accounts for 81.8%81.8\% of the eligible pool (385,770/471,876385{,}770/471{,}876); proportional sampling would make cross-site comparisons impossible. This design choice follows PRISM’s [27] per-country uniform-sampling strategy for cross-cultural balance.

Per-site composition.

The selected 2828 sites span Stack Exchange’s six categories with the distribution Technology 55, Science 77, Life & Arts 77, Culture & Recreation 66, Professional 22, Business 11. Table 4 reports for each site the official category, audience description (verbatim from the Stack Exchange Sites API), pool size after Step 5 of the quality filter, sample size (400400 uniform), and mean posting year. The mean year across the full pool is 2020.272020.27, indicating that the dataset reflects the period when search-augmented LLMs entered mainstream use.

B.2 Collecting Search-Augmented Responses and Extracting Citations

Model selection.

We select ten search-augmented LLMs from five major providers, including standard/reasoning variant pairs to enable controlled comparisons of reasoning effects on citation behavior. GPT-5 and GPT-5 mini (OpenAI), Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic), Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google), Grok 4.1 Fast-Non-Reasoning and Grok-4.1 Fast-Reasoning (xAI), and Sonar and Sonar Reasoning Pro (Perplexity). Selection criteria are: (i) provider diversity to capture distinct retrieval-backend behaviors, (ii) built-in search tool support via the production API, (iii) non-deprecated availability throughout the collection window, and (iv) the existence of at least one standard/reasoning pair within each provider that supports such pairing. Table 5 summarizes per-model API parameters, search tools, and collection windows.

Prompt design.

We use a single system prompt across all ten models to isolate citation behavior specific to each model from variance introduced by the prompt. The prompt is designed to intervene as little as possible, providing no specification of citation format, count, or preference for particular source types so that each model’s natural citation behavior can surface. At the same time, it preserves a realistic query format by passing only the Stack Exchange post title as the user query, mimicking the short questions users typically ask rather than inputs that have been artificially expanded. The full system prompt appears in Figure 6.

Response collection.

We dispatch each of the 11,20011{,}200 queries to each of the 10 models, yielding 11,200×10=112,00011{,}200\times 10=112{,}000 responses. All collection occurs within the same 1515 days to limit temporal drift in the live web index that each provider’s search tool consults. Rate limits on the provider side, transient errors, and timeout retries are handled via exponential backoff with a maximum of three retries per call. Calls that fail all three retries are logged with an empty response body and excluded from downstream analysis.

Citation extraction and normalization.

The five providers return citations in five different API formats, summarized in Table 6. We parse each format and normalize all citations to a common schema ⟨cited_sentence,source_url⟩\langle\texttt{cited\_sentence},\texttt{source\_url}\rangle, where cited_sentence is the portion of the answer that relies on the source and source_url is its URL. For providers that use inline markers (OpenAI, xAI, Perplexity), we extract a context window of two sentences around each marker, which aligns with the citation blocks of 11 to 22 sentences that Anthropic and Google return directly. After normalization we obtain 1,271,0461{,}271{,}046 citation pairs across the full 112,000112{,}000 responses. 8,0698{,}069 responses contain no citations and are excluded from evaluation on individual dimensions but retained in the public release.

Extraction reliability.

For providers that return citations as structured blocks (Anthropic, Google), extraction is deterministic because the API returns JSON fields (cited_text, source_url) that require no heuristic parsing. For providers that use inline markers (OpenAI, xAI, Perplexity), the context window of two sentences captures more than the minimum grounding context, so fidelity judgments (Answer-Source Fidelity, §C.3) remain conservative. A wider window may include text that is not grounded but will not miss the grounded claim. Residual parsing failures such as truncated sentences or malformed markers produce defective cited_sentence entries. These entries are caught by the evaluability filters in §B.3, which remove code or table content, overly short extractions, and entries under five words before evaluation on individual dimensions.

B.3 Crawling and Verifying Source Content

Pipeline.

Each unique URL extracted from citations is processed through a pipeline of four stages. First, we resolve redirects (e.g., Gemini proxy URLs) and strip tracking parameters to obtain the canonical URL. Second, we render the page using a headless browser (Playwright Chromium), falling back to an async HTTP client when rendering fails. Third, we convert the retrieved HTML to plain text, applying trafilatura [6], readability-lxml,, and raw innerText as successive fallbacks to maximize extraction coverage. Finally, we detect error pages by checking whether the extracted text is too short or matches known patterns for bot blocking. All crawling respects robots.txt and enforces rate limiting per domain[29]. Table 7 lists the specific thresholds and timeout values used at each stage.

Crawl results.

The pipeline successfully retrieves 231,105231{,}105 of 396,670396{,}670 unique URLs (58.3%58.3\%), covering 63.2%63.2\% of all citation pairs (Table 8). The most common reasons for failure are JavaScript rendering or bot blocking and documents in formats other than HTML such as PDF (Table 9). Failures are not uniform across host types. Forum and Q&A hosts fail most often, primarily due to Cloudflare bot blocking, while news domains have the highest success rate (Table 10). As a result, community and personal sources are underrepresented in the evaluable pool. For example, the share of forum and Q&A sources drops from 16.6%16.6\% of all sources to 8.6%8.6\% after crawling. We therefore treat our SFR estimate as a conservative lower bound, as discussed further in Appendix D.6 and Section 4.

Evaluability filtering.

Among the 802,945802{,}945 successfully crawled citations, we apply four filters to exclude pairs whose cited_sentence is defective. Following the staged attrition protocol of CiteME [42], we report each filter’s effect separately rather than as a single aggregate (Table 11). The filters remove sentences that consist solely of code or table fragments, sentences flagged as unevaluable by the LLM judge, and sentences that are too short in character length or word count, accounting for 5.22%5.22\% of the crawled pool. The final evaluable set contains 761,495\mathbf{761{,}495} citation pairs across the ten models. Evaluable rates per model range from 85.2%85.2\% (Gemini 3 Flash) to 99.3%99.3\% (Claude Sonnet), with variation largely due to differences in how often each model produces code in its citations (Table 12). All metrics in Appendix D are computed on this filtered pool.

Appendix C Three-Dimension Evaluation Framework

This appendix expands the evaluation framework summarized in Section 3. Following the structure of the main text, we describe Intent–Purpose Alignment in §C.1, Source Suitability in §C.2, and Answer–Source Fidelity in §C.3. For each dimension we present the taxonomy, the scoring rubric, the aggregation method at the response level, and the supporting validation evidence. Integration across dimensions and robustness checks are covered in §C.4. Each dimension is built from one or two underlying classification tasks: Query Intent (QI) and Source Purpose (SP) for alignment, Source Domain (SD) and Source Type (ST) for suitability, and Answer–Source Fidelity (ASF) for fidelity.

Judge configuration.

All five classification tasks use a single LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18), called with temperature 0, strict JSON-mode structured output, and a 4,0964{,}096-token output limit. The full prompt for each task appears in Figures 7 through 10.

C.1 Alignment Between Query Intent and Source Purpose

Query Intent (QI) taxonomy.

Query Intent classifies each query by its primary completion condition [55, 11, 22], defined as what the user must obtain to consider the query resolved. We define five labels (Table 13): QI1 Factoid (single verifiable datum), QI2 Explanation (causal mechanism or principle), QI3 Instruction (procedural steps or troubleshooting), QI4 Comparison (evaluation of alternatives), and QI5 Opinion (subjective or value-laden judgment), extending NF-CATS [10, 46, 23] with a dedicated comparison category (QI4) that prior work conflates with instruction.

Source Purpose (SP) taxonomy.

Source Purpose classifies each cited source by its communicative function [7, 50, 52], defined as the goal that the source’s author pursues regardless of factual content. We define six labels (Table 14): SP1 To Promote (commercial advocacy), SP2 To Inform (neutral knowledge transmission), SP3 To Instruct (procedural guidance), SP4 To Report (event reporting), SP5 To Discuss (community deliberation), and SP6 To Opine (individual perspective). This distinction matters because the purpose of a source shapes its structural incentive: a promotional source may present accurate facts yet frame them to favor a product, creating a mismatch when paired with informational queries.

IPA matrix design.

The Intent–Purpose Alignment(IPA) Matrix is a 5×65\times 6 matrix that scores each (QI, SP) combination on a 11–55 scale (Table 15). For a citation pair c=(q,ac,sc)c=(q,a_{c},s_{c}) classified as QI⁡(q)\mathrm{QI}(q) and SP⁡(sc)\mathrm{SP}(s_{c}), the alignment score is

IPA⁡(c)=𝐌I​P​[QI⁡(q),SP⁡(sc)]∈{1,2,3,4,5}.\mathrm{IPA}(c)=\mathbf{M}_{IP}[\mathrm{QI}(q),\,\mathrm{SP}(s_{c})]\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}. (1)

Scores of 33–55 indicate functional alignment, where the source’s communicative function contributes to the query’s completion condition (55 = direct match, 33 = partial relevance). Scores of 11–22 indicate structural misalignment, where the source’s incentive conflicts with the query’s information need (11 = structural conflict, 22 = weak fit). We define citations with IPA⁡(c)≤2\mathrm{IPA}(c)\leq 2 as alignment failures. This threshold corresponds to the boundary between the two regimes in the rubric, and we verify in Appendix D.6 that shifting the threshold by ±1\pm 1 preserves relative model rankings. Per-cell justifications appear in Table16–17.

Response-level aggregation.

For a response rr with citation set CrC_{r}, we define two metrics:

R-IPA(r)=1|Cr|∑c∈CrIPA(c),AFR(r)=|{c∈Cr:IPA⁡(c)≤2}||Cr|,\mathrm{R\text{-}IPA}(r)=\frac{1}{|C_{r}|}\sum_{c\in C_{r}}\mathrm{IPA}(c),\qquad\mathrm{AFR}(r)=\frac{|\{c\in C_{r}:\mathrm{IPA}(c)\leq 2\}|}{|C_{r}|}, (2)
R-AFR(r)=𝟙[∃c∈Cr:IPA(c)≤2].\mathrm{R\text{-}AFR}(r)=\mathbbm{1}\bigl[\exists\,c\in C_{r}:\mathrm{IPA}(c)\leq 2\bigr]. (3)

R-IPA is the mean alignment score per response (higher is better), AFR (Alignment Failure Rate) is the share of citations in the conflict region (lower is better), and R-AFR (Response-level Alignment Failure Rate) is a binary indicator of whether the user encounters at least one misaligned citation in the response. Responses with zero citations (10.3%10.3\% of the corpus) are excluded from aggregation but retained in the public release.

Validation.

A panel of 1010 IR/LIS researchers independently rated all 3030 IPA Matrix cells on a 11–55 scale. Inter-rater reliability is excellent (ICC⁡(2,k)=0.916\mathrm{ICC}(2,k)=0.916 [28], 95%95\% CI =[0.86,0.95]=[0.86,0.95]), and the correlation between expert consensus and design values is strong (r=0.871r=0.871, CCC=0.821\mathrm{CCC}=0.821). No cell deviates from expert consensus by 22 or more points, and the four cells with 11-point deviation are all in the conservative direction. Full validation statistics appear in Table 24. On the QI (κ=0.862\kappa=0.862) and SP (κ=0.862\kappa=0.862) label-assignment tasks, the LLM judge reaches substantial agreement against three human annotators (Table 26).

C.2 Source Suitability Across Domains and Types

Source Domain (SD) taxonomy.

SD classifies each cited source by the substantive domain of its content into ten labels [21] (Table 18): SD1 Medical (diseases, treatments, mental health), SD2 Legal (law, regulation), SD3 Finance (banking, taxation), SD4 Education (curriculum, university, scholarship), SD5 Science (natural science, research), SD6 Code/Data (software, datasets), SD7 Technical (engineering, specifications), SD8 Social/Professional (workplace, career), SD9 Shopping/Travel (commerce, lifestyle purchases), and SD10 Everyday (recipes, hobbies, routine information). Labels SD1–SD3 correspond to the YMYL domains identified by Google’s Search Quality Rater Guidelines [17]; SD4–SD7 capture knowledge-intensive domains; SD8–SD10 capture lifestyle and routine information.

Source Type (ST) taxonomy.

ST classifies each source by its publication infrastructure and editorial accountability [45, 51] into six labels (Table 19): ST1 Official (government, regulatory agencies, nonprofits), ST2 Research (peer-reviewed academic publication), ST3 News (mainstream journalism), ST4 Wiki/Forum (community-edited or community-discussion content), ST5 Blog/Social (individual-author or social-media content), and ST6 Company (corporate or commercial content). This is distinct from SP, which captures communicative intent rather than institutional structure.

SS matrix design.

The Source Suitability (SS) Matrix is a 10×610\times 6 matrix scoring each (SD, ST) combination on a 11–55 scale (Table 20). For citation pair c=(q,ac,sc)c=(q,a_{c},s_{c}) with source scs_{c}, the suitability score is

SS⁡(c)=𝐌S​S​[SD⁡(sc),ST⁡(sc)]∈{1,2,3,4,5}.\mathrm{SS}(c)=\mathbf{M}_{SS}[\mathrm{SD}(s_{c}),\,\mathrm{ST}(s_{c})]\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}. (4)

Cell values follow the CRAAP test [8] for source evaluation and the YMYL classification [17], governed by two principles. First, in YMYL domains (SD1–SD3), only Official and Research sources receive 55, while Wiki/Forum and Blog/Social receive 11 in Medical and Legal domains due to the risk of unverified information in high-stakes contexts. Second, in Code/Data (SD6), Wiki/Forum sources (ST4) receive 55 because developer communities such as Stack Overflow hold de facto authority in software engineering; this reflects the empirical authority structure of the domain rather than a deviation from the CRAAP framework. In non-YMYL domains (SD9 Shopping/Travel, SD10 Everyday), the minimum cell value is 33 rather than 11, reflecting the lower stakes of misalignment in routine contexts. We define citations with SS⁡(c)≤2\mathrm{SS}(c)\leq 2 as suitability failures, and verify in Appendix D.6 that shifting the threshold by ±1\pm 1 preserves relative model rankings. Per-cell justifications appear in Tables 21–23.

Response-level aggregation.

For a response rr with citation set CrC_{r}, we define two metrics:

R-SS(r)=1|Cr|∑c∈CrSS(c),SFR(r)=|{c∈Cr:SS⁡(c)≤2}||Cr|.\mathrm{R\text{-}SS}(r)=\frac{1}{|C_{r}|}\sum_{c\in C_{r}}\mathrm{SS}(c),\qquad\mathrm{SFR}(r)=\frac{|\{c\in C_{r}:\mathrm{SS}(c)\leq 2\}|}{|C_{r}|}. (5)
R-SFR(r)=𝟙[∃c∈Cr:SS(c)≤2].\mathrm{R\text{-}SFR}(r)=\mathbbm{1}\bigl[\exists\,c\in C_{r}:\mathrm{SS}(c)\leq 2\bigr]. (6)

R-SS is the mean suitability score per response (higher is better), SFR (Suitability Failure Rate) is the share of citations from unsuitable source types for the relevant domain (lower is better), and R-SFR (Response-level Suitability Failure Rate) is a binary indicator of whether the user encounters at least one unsuitable source in the response. Responses with zero citations are excluded from aggregation but retained in the public release.

Validation.

A panel of 100100 domain experts (1010 per domain) independently rated the 66 cells of their assigned domain on a 11–55 scale. SD1–SD7 were rated by domain professionals or researchers, and SD8–SD10 by graduate-level researchers. Inter-rater reliability is excellent across domains (99 of 1010 domains with ICC⁡(2,k)≥0.90\mathrm{ICC}(2,k)\geq 0.90 [28], median =0.958=0.958), and the correlation between expert consensus and design values is strong (r=0.943r=0.943, CCC=0.934\mathrm{CCC}=0.934). No cell exhibits Tier 11 disagreement (≥2\geq 2 points from expert consensus). Full per-domain statistics appear in Table 24.

C.3 Fidelity of Answers to Their Sources

Answer–Source Fidelity (ASF) taxonomy.

The ASF taxonomy classifies the relationship between a citing sentence and the crawled source content on a 11–55 scale (Table 25): ASF5 Supported (every claim attributable to the source), ASF4 Amplified (claims attributable but a critical qualifier omitted), ASF3 Contradicted (a hedged claim presented as unconditional or reversed), ASF2 Misattributed (the source provides only tangential evidence), and ASF1 Fabricated (no claim supported by the source). The taxonomy extends the binary supported/not-attributable judgment of ALCE [16] and AIS [44, 36, 41, 31, 58, 32]; the three intermediate levels (ASF4–ASF2) capture the directional distortions characteristic of Verified Misguidance.

Citing sentence and source content.

Each citation pair consists of a two-sentence cited unit extracted from the model’s response and the corresponding crawled source content. The extraction procedure for both marker and block providers is described in Appendix B.3. The ASF judge receives both the cited unit and the source content, and assigns one of the five verdicts (ASF1–ASF5).

Response-level aggregation.

For a response rr with citation set CrC_{r}, we define two metrics:

FFR(r)=|{c∈Cr:ASF⁡(c)≤2}||Cr|,R-FFR(r)=𝟙[∃c∈Cr:ASF(c)≤2].\mathrm{FFR}(r)=\frac{|\{c\in C_{r}:\mathrm{ASF}(c)\leq 2\}|}{|C_{r}|},\qquad\mathrm{R\text{-}FFR}(r)=\mathbbm{1}\bigl[\exists\,c\in C_{r}:\mathrm{ASF}(c)\leq 2\bigr]. (7)

FFR (Fidelity Failure Rate) is the share of citations that fail (lower is better), and R-FFR (Response-level Fidelity Failure Rate) is a binary indicator of whether the user encounters at least one failed citation in the response. The threshold ASF⁡(c)≤2\mathrm{ASF}(c)\leq 2 groups Fabricated (ASF1) and Misattributed (ASF2), both of which share the property that a user examining the source cannot independently verify the cited claim, distinguishing them from Contradicted (ASF3) or Amplified (ASF4) cases where the source contains the claim in some form. Responses with zero citations are excluded from aggregation but retained in the public release.

Validation.

The LLM judge’s ASF classification was validated against three human annotators on 200200 stratified samples (140140 from a base split with 1010 Supported and 44 Fabricated cases per model, plus 6060 samples covering the three intermediate subtypes at 2020 each) to ensure adequate coverage of rare failure categories. Cohen’s κ\kappa [12] against majority vote consensus is 0.8580.858 (95%95\% CI =[0.789,0.914]=[0.789,0.914]), indicating excellent agreement, with balanced accuracy of 0.9180.918. Agreement among the three human annotators is Krippendorff’s α=0.811\alpha=0.811 [30] (all pairwise κ≥0.802\kappa\geq 0.802), exceeding the substantial agreement threshold [33] (α≥0.667\alpha\geq 0.667). Full reliability statistics for all five dimensions appear in Table 26.

C.4 Cross-Dimension Integration and Robustness

Critical VM definition.

We define a citation pair as a Critical VM instance when all three dimensions fail simultaneously:

CritVM(c)=𝟙[IPA(c)≤2∧ASF(c)≤2∧SS(c)≤2].\mathrm{CritVM}(c)=\mathbbm{1}\bigl[\mathrm{IPA}(c)\leq 2\;\wedge\;\mathrm{ASF}(c)\leq 2\;\wedge\;\mathrm{SS}(c)\leq 2\bigr]. (8)

Each individual dimension condition corresponds to an established evaluation framework: Intent–Purpose Alignment to query intent taxonomies such as NF-CATS [10], Source Suitability to source quality frameworks such as CRAAP [8], and Answer–Source Fidelity to citation verification benchmarks such as ALCE [16] and CiteME [42]. The simultaneous failure across all three is not captured by any single existing framework, and this composition across dimensions is the central evaluative contribution of CiteTrace.

Statistical independence test.

Under the null hypothesis that the three dimensions fail independently, the expected joint failure rate is the product of the marginal rates:

𝔼indep​[CritVM]=AFR⋅FFR⋅SFR=0.051⋅0.306⋅0.271≈0.0042=0.42%.\mathbb{E}_{\text{indep}}[\mathrm{CritVM}]=\mathrm{AFR}\cdot\mathrm{FFR}\cdot\mathrm{SFR}=0.051\cdot 0.306\cdot 0.271\approx 0.0042=0.42\%. (9)

The observed CritVM rate is 3,174/761,495=0.42%3{,}174/761{,}495=0.42\%, matching the independent failure expectation. A formal χ2\chi^{2} test against full pairwise dependence is reported in Appendix D.6.

Single judge dependence.

All five classification dimensions use a single LLM judge (GPT-4o-mini). This is consistent with the evaluation methodology of comparable frameworks: ALCE [16] validates citation quality against a single NLI model (κ=0.525\kappa=0.525), RAGAS [14] prompts a single LLM, and ARES [47] trains a single tailored judge per dimension. Our κ\kappa values (0.7960.796–0.8620.862, Table 26) substantially exceed these baselines, and the stratified validation protocol (§C.3) with three independent human annotators (Krippendorff α≥0.811\alpha\geq 0.811) provides strong evidence that the judge’s classifications are reliable. Nonetheless, absolute metric values may shift under judge replacement; we discuss this dependence in Appendix A and encourage replication with alternative judge families.

Threshold sensitivity protocol.

The failure threshold ≤2\leq 2 for all three dimensions is anchored in the conflict and failure regime built into the rubrics (§C.1, §C.2, §C.3). To quantify sensitivity to this choice, we evaluate seven ±1\pm 1 perturbation variants across the three dimensions: {<2,≤2,≤3}\{<2,\leq 2,\leq 3\} for each dimension independently, plus four mixed perturbations. Rankings preserve Kendall τ≥0.82\tau\geq 0.82 in five of the seven variants, with the two exceptions involving the ≤3\leq 3 perturbation of Answer–Source Fidelity (FFR), which compresses the spread across models but retains the overall provider ordering. Full ranking tables for each variant appear in Appendix D.6.

Appendix D The VM Effect: Detailed Empirical Results

This appendix expands the empirical results summarized in Section 4. Seven subsections organize the material from the broadest aggregate view to fine-grained robustness checks: structural composition of the source pool (§D.1), aggregate failure rates across the three evaluation dimensions (§D.2), the fidelity–suitability trade-off across models (§D.3), how provider, scale, and reasoning shape citation quality (§D.4), response-level failure exposure (§D.5), robustness and lower bounds (§D.6), and qualitative failure analysis (§D.7). All metrics are computed on the final evaluable pool of 761,495 citation pairs (Appendix B.3, Table 11).

D.1 A Structurally Biased Source Pool

Source pool composition.

The pool of sources from which models cite is structurally skewed before any dimension-level failure occurs (Table 27). The skew concentrates on what kind of source the models choose (Source Type) and what those sources are written for (Source Purpose); the domains those sources cover are, in contrast, distributed nearly uniformly. The two largest Source Types are Blog/Social (29.2%) and Private Company (21.1%): community-edited and corporate sources together account for about half of all citations (50.3%), nearly twice the 26.3% from Official Institution (17.5%) and Paper/Research (8.8%) combined. Source Purpose is even more concentrated: To Inform (73.1%) and To Instruct (17.1%) together account for 90.2% of all citations, while the four remaining purposes (To Discuss 4.9%, To Promote 2.5%, To Report 1.6%, and To Opine 0.8%) collectively make up only 9.8%. Source Domain, by contrast, is approximately uniform across the seven leading domains, ranging from Technical (14.1%) down to Legal (10.5%) within a four-point spread; the high-stakes YMYL domains, comprising Medical/Health, Legal, and Finance, together accounts for 34.9% of all citations.

D.2 Aggregate Failure Rates Across Three Dimensions

The 761,495 evaluable citations admit three orthogonal failure modes, one per dimension: Intent–Purpose Alignment, Source Suitability, and Answer–Source Fidelity. The aggregate Fidelity Failure Rate (FFR) of 30.6% on Answer–Source Fidelity is the largest of the three; the Suitability Failure Rate (SFR) of 27.1% on Source Suitability is comparable; the Alignment Failure Rate (AFR) of 5.1% on Intent–Purpose Alignment is an order of magnitude smaller.

Answer–Source Fidelity.

The fidelity distribution is sharply bipolar: 61.2% Supported, 24.5% Fabricated, 14.3% intermediate. The aggregate FFR is 30.6%, with mean ASF = 3.74 (SD = 1.73). When fidelity fails, it tends to fail outright rather than partially.

Source Suitability.

Scores concentrate around Borderline (score 3, 33.3%) but unlike fidelity show no bipolar gap. The failure region (scores 1–2) accounts for 27.1%: Weak Mismatch (21.5%) and Severe Mismatch (5.6%). Most suitability failures are marginal rather than catastrophic—a source one step removed from the ideal type rather than wholly inappropriate. The aggregate SFR (SS ≤\leq 2) is 27.1%, with mean SS = 3.32 (SD = 1.22).

Intent–Purpose Alignment.

The alignment distribution is concentrated at score 5 (63.2%), with score 3 as a secondary mode (20.5%) and only 5.1% in the failure region (scores 1–2). Mean IPA = 4.31 (SD = 1.01). The low failure rate reflects the makeup of the source pool: Inform-purpose sources account for 73.1% of all citations and score 4 or 5 against the two most common query intents (Explanation 44.8%, Factoid 18.4%).

Three-dimension summary.

The three dimensions differ not only in failure rates but in what drives them (Table 29). Answer–Source Fidelity has the highest failure rate (FFR 30.6%) and the largest model effect (ηH2=0.087\eta^{2}_{H}=0.087, medium); Source Suitability has a slightly lower aggregate rate (SFR 27.1%) but is the most domain-sensitive dimension, with YMYL SFR nearly doubling the non-YMYL rate (Table 30); Intent–Purpose Alignment has the lowest rate by an order of magnitude (AFR 5.1%) and is the least consequential for aggregate citation quality. The three dimensions capture distinct phenomena rather than a single quality factor, as confirmed by the independence test in §D.6.

D.3 The Fidelity–Suitability Trade-off Across Models

Answer–Source Fidelity is model-driven.

Disaggregating to the model level reveals a 3.6-fold FFR spread: claude-haiku at 12.3% versus gpt-5-mini at 44.9% (Figure 15). A Kruskal–Wallis decomposition assigns ηH2=0.087\eta^{2}_{H}=0.087 (medium effect; H=66,265H=66{,}265, p<0.001p<0.001) to model identity but only ηH2=0.002\eta^{2}_{H}=0.002 (negligible) to query category, a 45-fold ratio (Table 29). Fidelity failure is driven almost entirely by model identity rather than by query category.

Source Suitability partly inverts the fidelity ranking.

SFR ranges from 8.0% (gpt-5) to 33.5% (gemini-3-flash), a 4.2-fold spread (Table 31). The Kruskal–Wallis model effect (ηH2=0.041\eta^{2}_{H}=0.041, small) is weaker than for fidelity but still exceeds the category effect (ηH2=0.026\eta^{2}_{H}=0.026): source suitability, too, is model-determined. Yet the ranking partly inverts the fidelity ranking: the Anthropic models, top-ranked on FFR (ranks 1–2), drop to SFR ranks 7 and 9, while gpt-5 holds SFR rank 1 despite FFR rank 8. The rank shift Δ\Delta ranges from +8+8 (gpt-5-mini) to −7-7 (claude-sonnet), with every model above the inversion boundary exhibiting a corresponding SFR decline. This inversion sharpens further in YMYL domains (§D.2, Table 30).

Good citers pick bad sources.

The fidelity–suitability inversion traces to source selection: models with low FFR systematically draw from less authoritative source types (Table 32). gpt-5 concentrates 41.8% of its citations on Official sources and achieves the lowest SFR (8.0%); the Anthropic models route 32–35% into Blog and only 12% into Official, producing SFR above 30%. Company share remains near 21% across all models, so the cross-model SFR gap is driven almost entirely by the Official–Blog axis. Figure 16 plots each model’s FFR against its SFR: no model approaches the ideal corner, and models with similar source-type profiles occupy similar positions along the iso-failure contours, suggesting that the trade-off arises from the interplay between retrieval infrastructure and model-level source selection rather than from any single factor. The gap widens in YMYL domains (§D.2, Table 30).

D.4 How Provider, Scale, and Reasoning Shape Citation Quality

Providers exhibit structurally distinct profiles.

The five providers do not align on a single “citation quality” dimension but trade off across the three dimensions in structurally different ways (Table 33). Anthropic exhibits FFR = 12.9% and SFR = 31.3% (best fidelity, worst suitability); OpenAI exhibits FFR = 43.8% and SFR = 11.7% (worst fidelity, best suitability). Google and Perplexity cluster near the pool-wide mean on both dimensions, while xAI pairs high FFR (41.6%) with moderate SFR (24.7%). The Anthropic–OpenAI inversion documented at the model level in §D.3 thus extends to the provider level, consistent with each provider operating a distinct search infrastructure. The underlying score distributions (Figure 17) confirm that these rate differences reflect distinct distributional shapes rather than uniform shifts: Anthropic’s fidelity scores concentrate at 5 while OpenAI’s are bimodal, and the pattern reverses on suitability.

Provider identity dominates quality variance.

A two-way ANOVA decomposing per-dimension means by provider (between) and within-provider model confirms this pattern quantitatively (Table 34): provider effects account for 96.5% of IPA variance and 96.1% of SS variance, leaving under 4% for within-provider model differences. ASF variance is also provider-dominated at 88.3%, but the remaining 11.7% is attributable to within-provider model differences—roughly three times the residual of the other two dimensions. The asymmetry has a structural explanation: IPA and SS are determined by the retrieval backend alone, which fixes the source’s purpose and type before the generator sees them, so models sharing a backend score nearly identically. ASF depends also on how well the generator utilizes retrieved content, giving model-level language ability room to affect the outcome that the other two dimensions do not permit.

Larger models do not improve citation quality.

Within-provider model pairs that differ in scale but share a retrieval backend show marginal quality differences (Table 35). The Anthropic pair (sonnet versus haiku) differs by less than 0.8 pp on FFR and 1.6 pp on SFR despite sonnet issuing roughly twice as many citations per response. The OpenAI pair (gpt-5 versus gpt-5-mini) shows the largest within-provider gap: gpt-5 cites less and achieves both lower FFR (−-2.6 pp) and lower SFR (−-6.2 pp). The Google pair (pro versus flash) reproduces the D.3 trade-off in miniature: pro improves SFR by 3.5 pp but worsens FFR by 3.1 pp. In all three cases the within-provider Δ\Delta remains far smaller than the between-provider gaps of Table 33, confirming the 4–12% within-provider share reported above.

Reasoning improves only Answer–Source Fidelity.

The search-versus-generation decomposition can be tested directly using paired reasoning and non-reasoning models that share a retrieval backend (Table 36). The xAI pair (grok-4.1-fast (R) versus grok-4.1-fast (NR)) shows differences of at most 2 pp on all three dimensions—no measurable reasoning effect. The Perplexity pair (sonar-reasoning-pro versus sonar) shows a sharper pattern: the reasoning model issues half as many citations (8.2 versus 16.0 per query) while reducing FFR by 16.1 pp (18.0% versus 34.1%) and raising mean ASF by 0.65. But SFR and AFR differ negligibly (Δ\Delta SFR = +1.5 pp, Δ\Delta AFR = −-0.3 pp). When reasoning helps, it helps Answer–Source Fidelity only; source selection is governed by the search backend and is beyond the reach of generation-side improvements.

D.5 Response-Level Failure Exposure

Response-level failure exposure.

The metrics reported above are citation-level rates; the user-facing impact is at the response level, where any single failed citation constitutes user exposure (Table 37). For a model averaging n¯\bar{n} citations per response, even a modest citation-level rate compounds rapidly. Claude-sonnet’s FFR is only 13.1%, but with n¯=12.7\bar{n}=12.7 its response-level exposure (R-FFR) reaches 62.9%; its SFR of 31.7% produces R-SFR of 70.6%. The amplification is universal: the best-performing model (claude-haiku, n¯=5.3\bar{n}=5.3) still exposes 71.3% of its responses to at least one failure on any axis (Any), and models averaging n¯≥9\bar{n}\geq 9 exceed Any of 93%. The “good citers, bad sources” trade-off of §D.3 is not diluted but amplified at the response level: claude-sonnet achieves the second-lowest R-FFR (62.9%) yet the highest R-SFR (70.6%).

D.6 Robustness and Lower Bounds

Three dimensions are statistically independent.

The observed CritVM rate is 3,174 of 761,495 citations (0.42%), matching the independent-failure expectation AFR⋅FFR⋅SFR=0.051⋅0.306⋅0.271≈0.0042\text{AFR}\cdot\text{FFR}\cdot\text{SFR}=0.051\cdot 0.306\cdot 0.271\approx 0.0042 to two decimal places. The independence is not merely numerical but structural: each dimension is governed by a different factor. Answer–Source Fidelity is model-driven (ηH2=0.087\eta^{2}_{H}=0.087, medium); Source Suitability is model-driven but amplified by YMYL domains (ηH2=0.041\eta^{2}_{H}=0.041, OR = 2.32; Table 30); Intent–Purpose Alignment is category-driven (ηcat2=0.041\eta^{2}_{\text{cat}}=0.041), with Science queries achieving R-IPA 4.60–4.70 regardless of model while Professional queries fall to 4.00–4.47. Three different drivers produce three orthogonal failure modes. The Venn decomposition confirms this: ASF-only failures account for 22.2% of all citations, SS-only for 19.8%, and IPA-only for 2.2%, while the three-dimension intersection is 0.42%—at least 47 times smaller than even the smallest single-dimension bucket.

Threshold sensitivity.

Seven ±1\pm 1 perturbation variants of the ≤2\leq 2 failure threshold preserve model rankings at Kendall τ≥0.82\tau\geq 0.82 in five of seven cases (Table 38). The two exceptions are ss_strict (≤1\leq 1, τmodel=0.733\tau_{\text{model}}=0.733) and ipa_strict (≤1\leq 1, τmodel=0.644\tau_{\text{model}}=0.644), where the binary region is too sparse for stable rankings. Loosening the ASF threshold (asf_loose = ≤3\leq 3) preserves rankings most strongly (τ=0.956\tau=0.956); tightening ASF (asf_strict = ≤1\leq 1) preserves τ=0.911\tau=0.911. The reported threshold is a stable operating point.

Temporal stability.

Splitting the 15-day collection window at the median date (April 3, 2026) yields balanced per-dimension means with ≤\leq 5 pp shift; no model changes its rank-quartile assignment between halves (Table 39). The reported aggregate metrics are not the artifact of a single news cycle.

Crawl failures bias toward underestimation.

Of the 1,271,046 raw citation pairs, 36.8% failed to crawl (Appendix B.3, Table 8), and these failures are concentrated on Forum/Q&A (67.9% failure rate) and Blog/Social (55.0%) host tiers. Both tiers map onto SS cells with values ≤\leq 2 in YMYL domains. A second underestimation source is phantom citations: Google’s two models exhibit phantom-citation rates of 14.4–15.5% versus 2.1–5.0% for other models (Table 40), where the cited URL was never reachable; treating these as evaluation-eligible would worsen Google’s measured SFR and FFR. A third source is PDF-format citations: gpt-5 (16.8%) and sonar (15.4%) cite PDFs at substantially higher rates, and PDF failures are concentrated on Research and Official sources whose absence inflates measured SFR. The FFR, SFR, and AFR values reported throughout this appendix should be read as conservative lower bounds on the true population values.

D.7 Qualitative Failure Analysis

Overview.

Eight cases drawn from the CiteTrace corpus illustrate the failure typology at the single-citation and single-query level. Cases 1–2 exhibit all-three-fail CritVM patterns; Case 3 is a fully correct citation (all pass). Cases 4–5 isolate single-axis failures that expose the fidelity–suitability trade-off of §D.3: Case 4 shows a fabricated claim attributed to an authoritative source (ASF = 1, SS = 5), while Case 5 shows a faithful citation of an inappropriate source (ASF = 5, SS = 1). Cases 6 and 7 compare the same query across models and providers to show cross-provider divergence in source selection. Case 8 illustrates a phantom citation whose source was decommissioned between training and evaluation.

Appendix E Data Release and Reproducibility

We release CiteTrace as a static snapshot designed to support deterministic re-computation of every metric in Appendix D without re-querying provider APIs. The dataset is hosted on HuggingFace at https://huggingface.co/datasets/oseoko/citetrace-vm, with collection and analysis code at https://github.com/oseoko/verified-misguidance. This appendix specifies license terms (§E.1), the schema of the released tables (§E.2), and the boundary between what is and is not reproducible from the snapshot (§E.3).

E.1 Licensing

License terms.

Five license terms apply to different components of the release (Table 41). The query set inherits Stack Exchange’s CC BY-SA 4.04.0; research-original outputs are released under CC BY 4.04.0, and collection and analysis code under the MIT License. Crawling respected robots.txt and per-domain rate limits (§B.3); for redistribution we publish only source URLs and cited-sentence extracts, since per-domain ToS review across 231,105 unique URLs is infeasible.

Model-response redistribution.

At the collection date (2026−04−242026{-}04{-}24), each of the five providers’ (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, Perplexity) API Terms of Service grants response ownership to the API caller and does not prohibit academic redistribution of generated content; we have verified this provider-by-provider and reproduce the relevant ToS clauses in the dataset card. Reusers must attribute the originating provider and model and comply with each provider’s ToS at the time of reuse, which may differ from the terms in effect at our collection date.

E.2 Schema and Field Documentation

The analysis_master table.

The primary release artifact is analysis_master.parquet, containing 761,495761{,}495 rows, one per evaluable citation pair from the final pool. Table 42 documents all 2020 columns: each row carries the citation-pair identity (cit_id, query_id, model_short, url_id), the cited-sentence content, the five classification labels (QI_label, SP_label, ASF_label, SD_label, ST_label) with their derived scores (ipam_score, asf_score, ssm_score). This single table is sufficient to reproduce all aggregate metrics in Appendix D at both aggregation units used throughout the paper: citation-level (ncit=761,495n_{\text{cit}}=761{,}495, the row-level default) and response-level (nresp=86,788n_{\text{resp}}=86{,}788 after excluding zero-citation responses, grouped by (query_id, model_short)).

Auxiliary files.

Fourteen auxiliary files accompany analysis_master.parquet on the HuggingFace release (Table 43). The four parquet views flatten the same citation data into different analysis units (per-query, per-source, citation-only, and pre-extraction response), so secondary analyses can join along any axis without re-deriving keys. Seven human-evaluation tables release the validation studies underlying Appendix C: IPA and SS matrix-cell ratings (ipam/ssm, n=10n=10 raters per cell) and per-axis LLM-judge classification ratings (qi, sp, sd, st, asf; 200200 stratified samples ×\times 33 annotators per axis). The two scoring matrices (TSV) and the Stack Exchange site definitions (JSON) are reference inputs to the analysis pipeline; per-file schemas are documented in the Croissant manifest [3, 49] of the dataset card.

E.3 Reproducibility Notes

Two paths to reproducibility.

We provide two distinct paths to reproducibility, since bit-for-bit reproduction of the full pipeline is infeasible: each provider’s search tool issues live web queries during generation, so the source set returned for a given query depends on the search-index state at execution time, and running the collection script today against the same 11,20011{,}200 queries would yield a different response corpus. First, we redistribute the full collected corpus (response texts, cited-sentence extractions, source URLs, taxonomy labels, and matrix scores) so that all metrics in Appendix D can be reproduced deterministically without re-querying provider APIs. Second, the same pipeline (collection scripts, LLM-judge prompts, and the IPA and SS matrices) can be applied to new query sets, new models, or future re-collections, yielding analogous analysis_master-format outputs that the released reproduce.py can analyze.

Computational requirements.

Reproduction runs on a single CPU without GPU since the released artifact does not re-run model inference; library versions are pinned in requirements.txt.

API usage and token accounting.

Response collection issued 112,000112{,}000 API calls (11,20011{,}200 queries ×\times 1010 models) across five providers using each provider’s integrated search capability: OpenAI (gpt-5, gpt-5-mini), Anthropic (claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-haiku-4-5), Google (gemini-3.1-pro, gemini-3-flash), xAI (grok-4-1-fast reasoning and non-reasoning), and Perplexity (sonar-reasoning-pro, sonar). Source crawling attempted 435,411435{,}411 URLs, of which 231,105231{,}105 succeeded. LLM-judge classification issued 1,466,0101{,}466{,}010 calls to gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18: 693,315693{,}315 source-level (231,105231{,}105 sources ×\times 33 tasks), 11,20011{,}200 query-level (11,20011{,}200 queries ×\times 11 task), and 761,495761{,}495 citation-pair (761,495761{,}495 pairs ×\times 11 task). Total token usage is estimated at 2.72.7B input tokens and 190190M output tokens. Prompt development and pilot runs consumed additional tokens beyond the reported figures.
